Get started with zuspark

zuspark.Rmd

Spark Connect lets a client run Spark SQL on a remote cluster over gRPC, but every R route to it so far has gone through a JVM or a Python environment. zuspark speaks the protocol itself, so all you need to query a Spark Connect endpoint is R packages: connect, run SQL, and bring the result back as Arrow or as a data frame.

library(zuspark)

Connect

spark_connect() takes an sc:// connection string, by default the one in the SPARK_REMOTE environment variable. A local Spark Connect server listens on port 15002; this article runs against one.

con <- spark_connect()
con
#> <zuspark_connection> sc://127.0.0.1:15002 (Spark 4.2.1)
#>   session: 57995fad-632c-4e21-a8cb-034184cc012d
spark_version(con)
#> [1] "4.2.1"

Parameters go after a ;. token sends a bearer token and turns TLS on; any parameter zuspark doesn’t recognise is sent as a request header.

con <- spark_connect("sc://spark.example.com:443/;token=my-token")

For Databricks, spark_connect_databricks() builds the string and the header the workspace needs; see the Databricks article.

Run SQL

spark_sql() sends a statement. A query comes back as a zuspark_query, which holds the plan but no rows yet; nothing is read until you ask for it.

q <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT id, id * 2 AS twice, CAST(id AS STRING) AS s FROM range(5)")
q
#> <zuspark_query> SELECT id, id * 2 AS twice, CAST(id AS STRING) AS s FROM range(5)
#>   on sc://127.0.0.1:15002 (not run yet)

spark_schema() asks the server for the query’s types without running it. They are Spark’s types, as Spark names them.

spark_schema(q)
#>    name   type nullable
#> 1    id bigint    FALSE
#> 2 twice bigint    FALSE
#> 3     s string    FALSE

Commands such as DDL, DML and SET run at once, and spark_sql() returns the rows they produce as a data frame.

spark_sql(con, "CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW small AS SELECT * FROM range(3)")
#> data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows
spark_sql(con, "SHOW VIEWS")
#>   namespace viewName isTemporary
#> 1              small        TRUE

Collect the result

spark_collect() runs the query and returns one data frame. It runs it again every time, so the result is always current.

spark_collect(q)
#>   id twice s
#> 1  0     0 0
#> 2  1     2 1
#> 3  2     4 2
#> 4  3     6 3
#> 5  4     8 4

Values that R can’t hold exactly, such as a BIGINT beyond 2^53, are an error by default. lossy chooses their exact text or a widened type instead.

big <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT 9007199254740993 AS id")
conditionMessage(tryCatch(spark_collect(big), error = identity))
#> [1] "Column `id` (Arrow format `l`) can't be converted to R exactly: row 1 holds 9007199254740993. Load zuint to read it exactly, or use `lossy = \"character\"` for its exact text, or `lossy = \"allow\"` to accept the loss."
spark_collect(big, lossy = "character")
#>                 id
#> 1 9007199254740993
spark_collect(big, lossy = "allow")
#>             id
#> 1 9.007199e+15

spark_fetch() returns the result as an Arrow stream instead, for code that consumes Arrow directly, and spark_execute() runs a statement only for its effect, returning the number of rows it produced.

stream <- spark_fetch(q)
zuarrow::arrow_schema(stream)
#> <zuarrow_schema> struct<id: int64, twice: int64, s: string>
n <- spark_execute(con, "SELECT * FROM range(1000000)")
n
#> [1] 1e+06

Errors

Spark’s errors arrive as a zuspark_sql_error, with Spark’s error class and SQLSTATE. spark_error_details() asks the server for the rest.

err <- tryCatch(spark_sql(con, "SELECT * FROM no_such_table"), error = identity)
class(err)
#> [1] "zuspark_sql_error"     "zuspark_error"         "zugrpc_error_internal"
#> [4] "zugrpc_error_status"   "zugrpc_error"          "error"                
#> [7] "condition"
err$error_class
#> [1] "TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND"
err$sql_state
#> [1] "42P01"
details <- spark_error_details(err)
names(details[[1]])
#> [1] "type"               "message"            "error_class"       
#> [4] "sql_state"          "message_parameters" "cause"             
#> [7] "stack"              "contexts"
head(details[[1]]$stack, 3)
#>                                                            class
#> 1            org.apache.spark.sql.errors.QueryCompilationErrors$
#> 2 org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.analysis.package$AnalysisErrorAt
#> 3           org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.analysis.CheckAnalysis
#>                              method                         file line
#> 1 tableOrViewNotFoundWithSearchPath QueryCompilationErrors.scala  977
#> 2                     tableNotFound                package.scala   94
#> 3         $anonfun$checkAnalysis0$2          CheckAnalysis.scala  412

Settings, interrupts and disconnecting

spark_config() reads the session’s settings, or sets them by name and returns the values they had. An R interrupt (Ctrl-C, Esc) while a query runs stops it on the server; spark_interrupt() stops every operation of the session. spark_disconnect() releases the session.

old <- spark_config(con, spark.sql.session.timeZone = "UTC")
old
#> spark.sql.session.timeZone 
#>                  "Etc/UTC"
spark_config(con, "spark.sql.session.timeZone")
#> spark.sql.session.timeZone 
#>                      "UTC"
spark_interrupt(con)
spark_disconnect(con)
